I love PTA but didn't really think his latest film is all that is being made

Just saw One Battle After Another and even though the cinematography is masterful, as I would expect from PTA, I feel that if they had toned down the actions/chase scenes, the trademark DiCaprio quips, and instead fleshed out a bit more of Benicio's whole thing and let the storylines "brew" a bit more it could have been a way better film. This is where I think Licorice Pizza absolutely kills it—you don't have that many events to play with, so the rhythm of the film allows you to breathe in the themes much more. This is what Richard Linklater does to perfection. And even going back on PTA's work, for example There Will Be Blood, I feel this works way better because as a viewer you are confronting the ugly reality of the story in real time. I didn't get that with this latest one. I also think immigration is one of those topics that are so touchy right now, that there's no way in hell a film critic is gonna come out and look like they didn't like the pro-immigrant movie, and thus helps explain (in my opinion, I could be wrong) why it has received critical acclaim—while something like Licorice Pizza (that tackles some themes that can be seen as problematic, like the age gap difference between the characters) did not receive universal acclaim. Which is why I think most film criticism (the mainstream one, The Guardian and stuff like that) is just posturing. I like a film for what it accomplished as a film, not because I agree with its political message. In any way, I will watch everything PTA has to offer until the end. But just my two cents.

text: i'm a 'find the central metaphor' guy. but i'm enjoying the op's perspective and questions. one thing, though. you and op both talk about 'reducing' with this kind of analysis/interpretation. i personally feel the other way. that finding a central metaphor is a way for me to interrogate a thousand creative choices made by everyone on the movie. for me, i look closely at the million pieces of a movie to see how they fit together. and i can't think of another way to fit them together than they relate to a central metaphor. i'm not trying to be a contrarian. next time i watch a movie i'm going to ask myself OP's questions (*what kind of movement did this film take me through?, etc...)* before doing my usual central metaphor search. i just don't get the use of the word 'reducing'. I feel like i'm illuminating and airing the movie out in my mind when i contemplate a central metaphor. not for anybody else, just for myself.

text:
70's New Hollywood and the failure of the promise of streaming revolution

Despite being subscribed to 4-5 of the most common major streaming platforms in the U.S., lately I have been increasingly feeling like there's nothing to watch. "But how could that be true?" I have asked myself as I scroll through hundreds of titles across these various platforms. Typically each service will have a handful selection of all-time great movies, unfortunately many of which I have already seen. I considered maybe the problem is with me. But then this month I began reading Peter Biskind's "Easy Riders, Raging Bulls." For those not familiar, the book chronicles late 60's through the 70's Hollywood through the rise and fall of New Hollywood directors such as Coppola, Bogdanovich, Friedkin, Scorsese, etc. The book is lively and entertaining, but maybe a bit gossipy for my taste. Now of course when you consume a piece of media like that, you immediately want to revisit many of the films that are discussed in the work. However, I was completely shocked to discover just how few of these films are readily accessible through what I would call "Mainstream" movie streaming platforms. The following is a list of movies discussed in this book which are only available to watch through digital means via purchasing the films through digital download. They are not available to stream for free via a subscription on any platforms: * Bonnie and Clyde * Easy Rider * MASH * Five Easy Pieces * The Last Picture Show * McCabe and Mrs. Miller * Harold and Maude * The Godfather Part I & II * The King of Marvin Gardens * American Graffiti * Badlands * Mean Streets * The Exorcist * The Conversation * Chinatown * Nashville * Shampoo * Days of Heaven * Apocalypse Now * New York New York * Reds * Sorcerer * Being There This isn't meant to be exhaustive but illustrative, and there are many others that might be available only on ad-supported platforms making watching them akin to watching films on cable TV. I'm sure there are very complicated reasons why the streaming rights to a huge swath of Hollywood royalty are tied up in this or that deal. I also understand that all of the major streamers pivoted away from licensing other studio's movies to be able to spend billions producing their own dreck. I'm also aware that these rights differ by country, and things may look differently outside of the U.S. But this realization was damning to me. Especially as someone who came of age in a time when one could get almost an entire film education through a couple of streaming platforms. Now we have less great films available across 6-7 streaming services than we used to have across 1-2. This also isn't a call for a return to our roots in physical media like many would have it. For me personally the ship has sailed, I have neither the money nor the desire to house a physical movie collection. Luckily my local library has probably 80% of these movies on their shelf. Of course no one should ever rely on one company or one service to be able to provide a full lexicon for the history of film, but dammit this is not what we were promised. Streaming was supposed to usher in a new age of accessibility to old masters, and now directors like Altman, Bogdanovich, Coppola's entire careers are absent from where people go to consume movies. I can only assume this trend will continue and worsen.

What is a Cinephile?

What do you guys consider a cinephile? Many people here seem to watch more than 350+ movies a year and to me that’s really hard to do considering the time it will take. However, I love movies especially musicals and I would always sit down with my girlfriend to watch a movie almost every night ranging from Sharknado or the Meg 2 to War and Peace (1965 and 1956) and On Gaurd 1997, We do love classical musicals and classic movies like only Angels have wings or Rear Window and we also watch things like The Human Condition, YiYi, The Canes are flying but ofc average movies like Disney, Barbie, Batman animated movies, The Mummy, Club dread, Eurotrip etc, point is the range is just really large. But I think the range tends to stop at mostly experimental films like Dead Man’s Letters where it does start to show some avant-garde and especially when we get to films like La Flor, Out 1, Heimat we havnt seen those and it’s not something we’ll really sit through. I might try it cause I always try to be open minded and respect the work that’s put in but I do tend to lose my interest a little. Most I’ve seen was Napoleon 1927 and Shoah that were pretty long and that’s already pushing it. Movies like 964 Pinocchio just feel like I’m forcing myself to watch it jsut to see what it’s like to be a cinephile but I think we just loves movies but not sure if that makes us a cinephile? Silent films aren’t really my thing either but there are good ones. Other movies that are considered niche for me cause I don’t really hear anyone I know talking about them are; Valley of the Gwangi, The Bronx Warriors, Toy Soldiers, Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein, The Clan of the cave Bear, The Slipper and the Rose, Island of Love, Prince of Darkness, Phantom of the Paradise, Princess Tam Tam, Birth of a Nation, Gettysburg (which was really long), Gods and Generals, and Heart of Darkness: A filmmakers Apocalypse. I do love me some Nicolas cage weird movies too lol. I also have seen disturbing films like Serbian film and those I consider those to be on an other level than just horror. So, I really wonder am I just a movie buff rather than a cinephile because I don’t watch experimental films? I took a film class as a fun elective and that was it. A lot of the people in the class started talking about things like blaxploitation movies and I had no idea what they were but I did watch the movie *Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song 1971. I also like classic TV like* Have Gun Will Travel and the Dick Van Dyke Show. I hope this thread gives a little of my familiarity with cinema and movies and where I currently stand but again I do wonder would I be conserved just an above average movie watcher or movie buff rather than calling myself a cinephile? Or what makes a cinephile?

Dangerous Liaisons (1988) and Valmont (1989). One is better and more Dangerous than the other. Both had perfect casting.

I wish people would talk about Stephen Frears' Dangerous Liaisons (1988) more, which is an amazing and devastating film. But I think it's also a curiosity that Miloš Forman of all directors (having made Amadeus and One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest) made an inferior but still fascinating version of the same story (Valmont, 1989) with the same characters, released less than a year later. Something crazy is that they shot these films on location in France at the same time, with the cast and crew often interacting with one another. The casting for both films was incredible, and every actor nailed the role in different ways. Both are worth watching.
